newsitem.title: USA: UAL sees room to grow in U.S. market.
newsitem.headline: UAL sees room to grow in U.S. market.

text.p: UAL Corp said Friday that the domestic market still offers opportunities for its United Airlines to grow, in spite of intense competition in the U.S. airline industry.
"There is a view that the U.S. is a mature market," UAL Chairman Gerald Greenwald told reporters at a media briefing here. "Not for us."
For example, he said United could increase flights through the new Denver airport to 400 daily from 300 currently.
He declined to give a specific timeframe for expanding at Denver, which a United executive later said was the airline's most expensive airport.
Operating costs at Denver are 2.65 times that of United's average at other U.S. airports, said Rono Dutta, senior vice president of planning.
Meanwhile, at the main hub in Chicago, new technology could enable United to expand flights in the future by 15 to 20 percent, Greenwald said.
United continues to track the profitability of each of its routes, Greenwald said, adding it will phase out service that is not profitable and expand those that can pay for themselves.

No large expansion is seen for the Shuttle by United, the carrier's domestic service that flies short routes primarily on the West Coast, he said. The Shuttle has been expanded to 450 flights a day, as far east as Denver.
"We're doing just fine," Greenwald said. "However, we need to work to get our cost down further."
In overseas markets, Greenwald said he hoped for a more liberal bilateral agreement between the United States and the United Kingdom and a separate pact with Japan.
"I am less pessimistic about prospects of a more liberalized agreement" with Japan, Greenwald said.
Looking ahead, United, the world's largest airline based on revenue passenger miles flown, is looking to increase its profits by growing revenues, executive said.
The plan is "to grow our bottom line by focusing on our top line," Dutta said.
Part of that revenue growth is expected to come from targeting frequent business travelers for whom service takes priority over a cheap airfare, United executives said.

These business travelers make up only six percent of customers but account for 24 percent of United's flights and 37 percent of revenues, according to David Coltman, senior vice president of marketing.

Coltman acknowledged that United's newly unveiled advertising campaign, which carries the slogan "United is rising," does carry a risk since it promises to differentiate its service and improve performance.
But that risk is mitigated by the fact that United is taking actions now to improve customer satisfaction, including improved seats on existing aircraft not headed for retirement, he said.

John Edwardson, president and chief operating officer, added that "front-line" United employees, including flight attendants, have been given more authority to handle customer gripes, including giving out vouchers and coupons on the spot.
